subject: Indigenous Language

source.title: Junior School Curriculum Design: Indigenous Languages, Grade 9
source.notes: WebFetch could not extract text from the PDF directly but saved it locally; the Read tool then parsed the full PDF text natively (Claude's built-in PDF reader), not a WebFetch summary — every strand/sub-strand heading, SLO, KIQ, learning-experience bullet (including every parenthetical list), core competency, PCI, and Link-to-other-learning-area line below is transcribed verbatim from that read. Revised in 2024. Per the README's known-good sourcing pattern, this mirror copy was located via web search after the easylearn.co.ke Grade-9-specific URL guessed from the Grade 8 pattern could not be confirmed directly; the doyenpublishers.com URL above resolved to the authentic KICD document (title page, ISBN, and KICD branding all match). STRUCTURAL NOTE: unlike Grade 8's design (which is organised body-first around 9 themes-as-strands), the Grade 9 design's own front-matter 'SUMMARY OF STRANDS AND SUB STRANDS' table AND its body headings agree on a 3-strand structure — Listening and Speaking, Reading, Writing — each containing all 9 real-world themes as its sub-strands (matching this app's web/src/lib/curriculum.ts, which defines exactly il-listening-speaking / il-reading / il-writing as the 3 Grade 9 strands). This file therefore uses that 3-strand structure, not theme-as-strand. Content is generic-English-medium (grammar, comprehension and composition concepts) applied to indigenous-language-medium themes, not vocabulary in one specific mother tongue, since KICD's design is deliberately language-agnostic — confirmed both by the Essence Statement ('a people's culture is best passed on through their language... reasonable proficiency in the mother tongue... will be a prerequisite') and by every theme's 'Suggested Vocabulary' box listing only ENGLISH glosses (e.g. Theme 1: 'hero, heroine, community, save, serve...'), never target-language words. Lesson allocation per the front-matter table: Listening and Speaking 16, Reading 20, Writing 18, plus a separate 6-lesson 'Showcasing Concepts and Skills in Indigenous Language (Exhibitions)' entry not tied to any one theme = 60 total. This does not sum cleanly against the 9-themes x 2-lessons-per-substrand pattern actually used in the body (9x2=18 for every strand, not 16/20/18) — the document's own closing note under the summary table says 'The suggested number of lessons per Sub Strand may be less or more depending on the context,' so this is treated as an approximation in the front matter rather than a mining error. The Table of Contents in the source PDF omits 'THEME 6: ECONOMIC ACTIVITIES' from its listing (jumping from Theme 5 to Theme 7) but the theme's full 3-substrand body text (pages 31-36) is present and complete — a ToC typo, not a missing theme; captured in full below. The document also includes a 6-milestone Community Service-Learning (CSL) Appendix 1 (Problem Identification -> Designing a Solution -> Planning -> Implementation -> Showcasing/Exhibition -> Reflection) and an Appendix 2 table of suggested assessment methods / learning resources / non-formal activities per strand, both noted at top level below rather than per sub-strand since they are cross-cutting.

essenceNote: Per the design's own Essence Statement: 'Learners in Junior School will be exposed to a rich and supportive range of activities to develop indigenous language through the non-formal dimension... the indigenous language, like any other language, is central to the success or failure of education and development programmes... Reasonable proficiency in the mother tongue at this level will be a prerequisite for study of the subject at the Senior School level.' Subject General Learning Outcomes (by end of Junior School): (1) respond appropriately to a variety of communication in the indigenous language, (2) express themselves confidently and appropriately in a variety of social contexts, (3) demonstrate knowledge of and apply indigenous knowledge, culture and values in varied situations, (4) comprehend information in different contexts in the indigenous language, (5) read fluently and write legibly in different formats to express a variety of ideas and opinions, (6) enjoy communicating using a variety of cultural language strategies.

crossCuttingNotes.communityServiceLearningProject: Appendix 1: Grade 9 learners undertake an integrated, cross-subject Community Service-Learning (CSL) group project via a 6-step milestone approach staggered across the 3 terms: (1) Problem Identification (studying community challenges — environmental degradation, lifestyle/communicable/non-communicable diseases, poverty, violence and conflicts, food security), (2) Designing a solution, (3) Planning (roles, activities, resources, timelines), (4) Implementation (with evidence kept), (5) Showcasing/Exhibition and Report Writing, (6) Reflection (linking project work back to academic concepts). Coordinated by the Social Studies teacher across subjects; assessed formatively on skills applied, core competencies developed, and values nurtured. Not tied to any single Indigenous Language sub-strand — cross-cutting.
crossCuttingNotes.appendix2AssessmentAndResources: Appendix 2 lists, per strand: Listening and Speaking — oral narration, debates, public speaking, oral discussions/presentations, role plays, word games, oral reading, peer/self-assessment, dictation, aural tests; resources include dictionaries, newspapers, word walls/language corners, poetry books, flash cards, resource persons, plus digital sources (language games, songs, digital story books, recording devices, audio-visual resources); non-formal activities include debating sessions, club/society activities, community-event talks, composing/performing songs, mock interview panels, story-telling sessions during inter-class festivals. Reading — reading aloud, matching tasks, learner summaries, record of books read, portfolios, puzzles, mind maps; same resource list; non-formal activities include book clubs, poem recitation at school events, collecting community literature, spelling-bee contests, Pictionary sessions, language games. Writing — peer assessment, dictation, portfolio, anecdotal records, checklists/criteria, sentence construction; same resource list plus locally available materials for customised cultural objects; non-formal activities include dramatising/filming skits, composing poems in music/drama clubs, writing/compiling articles for magazines and clubs.

subStrands.notes: GAP FLAG: the shipped skill for this code (LS.3, il-ls-community-conjunctions-requests, web/src/skills/indigenousLanguage/communityConjunctionsRequests.ts, titled 'Serving the community: conjunctions and polite requests') does NOT match this sub-strand's actual PDF content. The design's 3.1.1 sub-strand is 'Pronunciation' — commonly mispronounced words and correct intonation/accentuation — not conjunctions or polite-request phrasing (that content belongs to Theme 4's negotiation sub-strand, 4.1.1, which IS correctly built as il-ls-negotiation-phrases). This is the one sub-strand across all 27 in this subject where the shipped skill's content diverges from its themed source text; every other LS/R/W code was cross-checked against the shipped skill title and content-matches cleanly. Recommend either retitling/rebuilding this skill to cover mispronounced-words + intonation, or building a companion skill for the missing content — flagged per CURRICULUM-MINING-GUIDE.md's 'nothing silently skipped' rule rather than silently accepted. PCI: Civic Responsibility. Values: Respect, Unity.

specificLearningOutcomes: identify the features of a poem for information
compose a short poem on the theme for creative expression
acknowledge the role of poetry in creating awareness on community service
keyInquiryQuestions: What makes a poem different from a story or a passage?
learningExperiences: work with peers to collect varied poems from the community
organise the poems collected in the class portfolio
conduct a reader's theatre to read poems on the theme
identify the features (e.g. poet, persona, stanzas and lines) in the poems
work jointly with peers to brainstorm ideas to consider when composing a poem on the theme — serving the community
work jointly with peers to compose a short poem on the theme and share for feedback
revise the poem based on the suggestions given by peers
display their best poems in the class gallery wall
join a club or society and initiate community service activities within the school environment

coreCompetencies: Creativity and Imagination — exchanging new ideas that inspire creativity when composing and sharing a short poem on the theme
Communication and Collaboration — working jointly with peers to brainstorm ideas to consider when composing a poem on the theme

subStrands.name: Essay writing
specificLearningOutcomes: explain the steps involved in writing a descriptive essay for information
write a descriptive essay for effective communication
recognise the role of writing on various topics for creative expression and enjoyment
keyInquiryQuestions: How can we describe events, people and things accurately?
How should one behave in public places to avoid putting others in danger?
learningExperiences: watch audio-visual clips on what to do in the event of an unforeseen disaster in a public place
make notes on the do's and don'ts in such scenarios
work with peers to use adjectives to describe a safe and unsafe public place
surf the internet or find publications on sample descriptive essays
discuss the parts of a descriptive essay (introduction, body, conclusion)
draft the introductory paragraph of a descriptive essay (280-320 words) related to the theme
share their work with peers for review
revise the essay based on feedback from peers
complete the descriptive essay and publish it in a school or public magazine
linkedLearningAreas: Pre-Technical Studies — the learner relates the skills on surfing the internet to access resources to online research
coreCompetencies: Communication and Collaboration — contributing to group decision making when using adjectives to describe a safe and unsafe public place
Digital Literacy — interacting with digital content when surfing the internet to find sample descriptive essays
subStrands.notes: PCI: Civic Responsibility (writing an essay on safety in public places and publishing it). Values: Responsibility, Patriotism.

subStrands.name: Creative Writing — Plays

write a short play based on the theme for communication
recognise the contribution of playwriting in the preservation of culture

work jointly with peers to discuss the features of a play with emphasis on the characters, setting language and stage directions
sketch a one-scene play related to the theme
exchange the play with peers for review
revise the script according to the suggestions given by their peers
write a two-scene play based on the theme
work with peers to allocate roles and act out the play
partner with peers to organise a class mini-festival and stage the plays
organise their best play scripts in the class portfolio

subStrands.name: Writing for information — Homonyms

distinguish meaning between homonyms for comprehension

Why do economic activities differ from one location to another?

construct sentences to clearly bring a distinction in meaning between homonyms
fill in gaps with correct words from a set of homonyms

share their work with peers for review

subStrands.name: Assessment of writing — Narrative Composition
specificLearningOutcomes: recognise the features of a well written composition for information
assess written texts for relevance, punctuation and neatness
acknowledge the need for quality in written work for effective communication
keyInquiryQuestions: How do you ensure quality of written work?
learningExperiences: search online and offline for features of a well written composition
work with peers to distinguish samples of neat and well written compositions from those that are not well written
outline common errors made when writing
work with peers to prepare a criteria or checklist for assessing written texts based on key features (e.g. relevance, punctuation, neatness)
write a short narrative composition on types of injuries sustained through road clashes and how to administer first aid
share their work with peers for assessment against the set criteria or checklist
review their written compositions based on feedback from peers
display their quality written work on the class gallery

coreCompetencies: Critical Thinking and Problem-solving — working with peers to analyse concepts when distinguishing neat/well written compositions from those that are not
Learning to Learn — motivated to learn continuously when working with peers to prepare a criteria/checklist for assessing written texts

subStrands.name: Creative writing — short story
specificLearningOutcomes: explain the features of a short story for information
write a short story featuring a hero or heroine for creative expression
recognise the place of short story writing in indigenous knowledge preservation
keyInquiryQuestions: How can we differentiate a short story from a novel?
Why is it important for a community to honour its heroes and heroines?
learningExperiences: read a short story from print or digital sources on community legends
work jointly with peers to examine the features of a short story
make notes on the features of a short story
identify a community or national hero and heroine and their unique qualities
prepare an outline of a short story featuring the community or national hero or heroine
use the outline to write a short story on the hero or heroine
share their story with peers for review
publish their refined short story in a school or public magazine
linkedLearningAreas: English — the learner relates the concept of writing short stories to their learning of the concept of creative writing
coreCompetencies: Digital Literacy — interacting with digital content when reading a short story from digital sources on community legends
Self-efficacy — showing concerted attention by using the outline to write a short story on the hero or heroine
subStrands.assessmentSignal: This sub-strand's plot/character-terms content (exposition/rising action/climax/falling action/resolution; character/setting/plot/conflict/theme) is not stated as a separate parenthetical list in the Suggested Learning Experiences column — it is inferred from 'examine the features of a short story' / 'make notes on the features of a short story' plus the general narrative-writing SLO. The shipped skill (shortStoryFeatures.ts) supplies these standard short-story-craft terms explicitly; treat as a reasonable, pedagogically standard operationalisation of 'features of a short story' rather than a verbatim-sourced list.
subStrands.notes: Cross-theme note: this W.8 sub-strand's suggested topic (a short story featuring 'a community or national hero and heroine') deliberately echoes Theme 1 (Community Heroes and Heroines) — a curriculum-sanctioned callback, not an accidental overlap. PCI: Social cohesion. Values: Patriotism, Respect.

subStrands.name: Functional Writing — Letters of application

write a letter of application for a scholarship for effective communication
acknowledge writing as a means of communicating for lifelong learning
keyInquiryQuestions: Why do we make applications whenever we need formal opportunities?
How do application letters differ from other letters?
learningExperiences: search online and offline for samples of scholarship application letters
work with peers to identify the components of a well written scholarship application letter
compose an application letter for a scholarship for Senior School education funding
share their written letters with peers for review
organize their reviewed letter in a portfolio
linkedLearningAreas: English and Kiswahili — the learner relates the concept of writing letters to similar concepts in functional writing
coreCompetencies: Communication and Collaboration — contributing to group decision making when identifying the components of a well written scholarship application letter
Digital Literacy — using digital technology to search online and offline for samples of scholarship application letters
subStrands.notes: The design specifies the scholarship is explicitly 'for Senior School education funding' — an application-letter skill should frame its scenario around Senior School transition funding specifically, not a generic scholarship, to match the source's intent. PCI: Human Rights. Values: Integrity, Responsibility.

assessmentRubricSummary.listeningAndSpeaking: Suggested Assessment Rubric (4 levels: Exceeding/Meeting/Approaching/Below Expectations) covers: Language in Use (parts of speech — nouns, pronouns, adjectives, prepositions, adverbs, verbs — in sentence construction), Listening for information (identifying target words, paraphrasing main idea/specific information), Listening for comprehension (inferring vocabulary meaning), Fluency (correct pronunciation, correct intonation, appropriate use of tongue twisters/riddles), Conversational skills (proper turn-taking and polite interruption during negotiations), Presentation skills (appropriate use of non-verbal cues — gestures, facial expressions, appearance, tonal variations, body movements — in public speaking, debates and storytelling).
assessmentRubricSummary.reading: Covers: Reading for comprehension (responding to direct/inferential questions, relating events/themes to real life), Library skills (effective library practices — silent reading, comprehension strategies, reading log), Reading for information (making connections between visuals and written texts), Intensive reading (applying pre-reading, note-making, inference, summarising strategies), Extensive reading (outlining main ideas from grade-appropriate texts).
assessmentRubricSummary.writing: Covers: Handwriting (neat, legible rewriting), Social and functional writing (emails, letters of application — correct format/language/organisation), Creative writing (poems, plays, short stories, descriptive essays — correct format/language/organisation), Assessment of writing (assessing handwritten texts for legibility, neatness, relevance, coherence).
